マルチタスクのパズルゲーム。だんだんと扱える列車を数が増えてくると自分自身の上手くやれている感があり満足できます。
割と難易度が高いように感じました。初めは1台を見ていればよいのですが、ステージ１の後半くらいから同時に2台見ないと間に合わなくなります。その後も難しくなってはいきますが、1台から2台になるこの辺りが一番、難易度上昇を感じました。ここを突破できればクリアまで行けると思うので、急に難しくなったと思っても、それはまだマルチタスクや操作に慣れていないだけなので繰り返し遊べばきっと慣れですんなりクリアできるようになると思います。

鉄道運行シミュレーターではなく、鉄道を題材にしたパズルゲームです。

限られた線路とホームをやりくりしながら、列車同士が衝突しないよう目的地へ送り届けます。時間が進む中、効率よくレールを敷き、ホームの空きを見て列車を出発させ、ポイントを切り替えていかに流れを作るかが本作の醍醐味です。

ステージが進むにつれて列車の本数が増え、忙しさも増していきます。鉄道の知識は不要で、状況を見ながら素早く判断するパズルゲームが好きな人にはおすすめです。

[h1]A Estação de Embarque: O Melhor Ponto de Partida[/h1]
[hr][/hr]

Se você quer entrar no mundo da gestão ferroviária, o primeiro [b]Train Valley[/b] é, sem dúvida, o melhor lugar para começar. Ele apresenta uma mecânica simples e intuitiva, acompanhada de um design visual belíssimo que o diferenciava totalmente de outros jogos de tráfego da época, como [i]Mini Metro[/i].

[b]Minha recomendação de ouro:[/b]
Comece por este jogo e pelo [b]Origins[/b]. Você certamente irá gostar da experiência de gerenciar trilhos e evitar as icônicas colisões de trens em um ambiente mais direto e focado.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Um aviso para os veteranos[/h2]

É importante destacar que, se você já jogou o [b]Train Valley 2[/b] ou o [b]Train Valley World[/b], sua percepção aqui pode ser diferente. Você pode acabar não gostando tanto deste primeiro título, pois ele [u]não possui a mesma complexidade[/u] dos seus sucessores.

Enquanto o 2 e o World introduziram camadas profundas de industrialização e processamento de materiais, o primeiro jogo foca no despacho de trens aleatórios. Para quem já está acostumado com cadeias de produção complexas, o gameplay aqui pode parecer um pouco simples demais.

[hr][/hr]
[b]Conclusão:[/b]
É uma joia para iniciantes e um clássico que definiu o gênero, mas pode parecer básico para quem já se tornou um mestre da logística nos títulos mais recentes.

[hr][/hr]
[spoiler] Aproveite para dominar a arte de evitar desastres ferroviários aqui antes de encarar a pressão industrial do segundo jogo! [/spoiler]

The OG Train Valley is a surprisingly compelling and challenging game. Goal is to get each train to the color-indicated station. Train Valley, developed by Alexey Davydov, Sergey Dvoynikov, Timofey Shargorodskiy, and the team at Flazm, is a clever and compact puzzle game that manages to combine the charm of model railroads with the challenge of strategic time and resource management. It places players in the role of a railway dispatcher, tasked with building efficient rail networks and managing train schedules across several eras and regions. With its clean art style, intuitive controls, and deceptively simple mechanics, Train Valley appeals both to puzzle enthusiasts and fans of train simulation, offering a gameplay experience that is easy to learn but increasingly difficult to master.

The core mechanic is straightforward: players must lay down track to connect stations and direct trains to their correct destinations without delay or collisions. However, beneath this simplicity lies a finely tuned system that requires forethought, timing, and spatial awareness. Trains appear with little warning and follow tight schedules, demanding quick decision-making and the ability to adapt to dynamic challenges. As the game progresses, the maps become more complex, with difficult terrain, tighter budgets, and overlapping routes forcing players to balance speed and safety. Mistakes can be costly—crashes result in penalties, and rerouting can become expensive if the wrong infrastructure is in place.

Train Valley features four main chapters—Europe, America, the USSR, and Japan—each with its own visual identity, historical references, and evolving train designs that reflect the era in which the levels are set. The inclusion of historical touchstones, such as the California Gold Rush or Cold War-era industrial growth, adds thematic richness, even if the game doesn't dive deep into narrative. Each level typically takes place in a different timeframe between the 19th and 21st centuries, subtly reflecting changes in technology and geography. While not essential to the gameplay, these touches contribute to a sense of progression and lend personality to what could otherwise be a purely abstract puzzle format.

Visually, the game is clean and colorful, with a charming, toy-like aesthetic that makes it feel like you’re managing a living model train set. Buildings, terrain, and trains are designed with clarity in mind, and the visual feedback is precise and helpful when making quick routing decisions. The camera offers flexible angles and zoom options, making it easy to keep track of the evolving railway landscape. Though the graphics aren’t particularly flashy, the overall presentation is polished and consistent, with a relaxing, pleasant art direction that keeps things engaging without visual clutter.

One of the most appealing aspects of Train Valley is the variety of game modes. In addition to the standard story campaign, which gradually introduces new mechanics and increases difficulty, there’s also a random level generator for extended replayability and a sandbox mode that allows for relaxed, unrestricted building without financial or time constraints. The sandbox feature is especially enjoyable for players who want to experiment with elaborate track systems or explore creative solutions without pressure. It allows for a more meditative experience, which contrasts nicely with the high-stakes challenge of the main campaign.

Despite its strengths, Train Valley does have a few limitations. The lack of depth in economic mechanics means that while the puzzle aspect is robust, fans of more intricate transport simulators might find it somewhat lacking. There's no cargo management system or industry growth mechanics like you’d find in larger-scale train sims. Additionally, later levels can sometimes feel frustrating due to the razor-thin margin for error—an early mistake in track planning or a misrouted train can quickly snowball into failure, requiring a complete restart. While this adds to the tension and challenge, it can also lead to moments of trial-and-error that some players might find discouraging.

That said, the game's balance between accessibility and depth is largely successful. The interface is intuitive, the controls are responsive, and the learning curve is gradual enough to accommodate a wide range of player skill levels. The scoring system encourages replayability, rewarding players who can find the most efficient and cost-effective solutions. The levels are designed to be relatively short—perfect for quick gaming sessions—but many will require multiple attempts to fully optimize, adding significant value and longevity to the experience.

Train Valley is ultimately a satisfying and well-crafted puzzle game that carves out its own space within the broader world of train and management sims. It doesn’t aim to be a sprawling logistics simulator; rather, it focuses on delivering tight, smart challenges wrapped in an aesthetically pleasing package. Whether you’re a fan of railroads, puzzles, or simply looking for a relaxing yet engaging game to sink some time into, Train Valley delivers a focused and enjoyable experience that is well worth a spot in any strategy lover’s library.

This feels like the beta version of Train Valley 2, containing some game elements that should have been redesigned or removed before releasing the final game. There are too many random elements like new stations appearing out of nowhere and destroying your existing tracks and trains, the whole design of the train scheduling feels unfinished and even the campain levels are randomly landscaped with every restart.
For Train Valley 2 they removed all the random elements and turned it into a optimisation game while Train Valley is all about dealing with random events. While I really like Train Valley 2 the prequel is similar but inferior to games like Flight Control or Mini Metro because here you spend much more time on your track layout only to be stopped by an unfair random element.
A game that entertains you and stresses you out at the same time, even with some achievements that are really hard to do.
